name: Organizational Leadership
notes: Could not open the official 2025-26 FBLA Organizational Leadership guideline: fbla.org returned HTTP 403 to every fetch (https://www.fbla.org/competitive-events/ and https://www.fbla.org/high-school/competitive-events/), and no PDF surfaced in search. Competency areas are therefore the standard high-school organizational leadership and management curriculum areas (leadership, motivation, communication, management functions, decision making, ethics, organizational structure and culture, change and conflict). The one partial reference found was a CliffsNotes page reproducing an archived 2018 FBLA-PBL Organizational Leadership competency list (https://www.cliffsnotes.com/study-notes/34046510), which I could not open to confirm. Re-check the sub areas and weights against the 2025-26 guideline PDF once it can be reached. Questions are original practice items written to FBLA state/NLC difficulty, with U.S. conventions. Verified 2026-10-11 (Omega answer-key pass): fbla.org still returned HTTP 403; a school news item (https://www.nhsd.org/o/nhshs/article/2328531) describes the event as covering leadership theories, organizational structures, team dynamics, decision making, and change management, which matches these sub areas.

questions.q: Which leadership style is characterized by the leader making decisions alone with little input from group members?
questions.explain: Autocratic leaders decide alone and direct followers. Democratic leaders seek member input, which is the common confusion.

questions.q: According to Maslow's hierarchy of needs, which level sits at the top of the pyramid?
questions.explain: Self-actualization is the highest level, reached after physiological, safety, belonging, and esteem needs are met.

questions.q: A manager openly admits a missed deadline and takes responsibility for fixing it with the team. Which core leadership trait is shown?
questions.explain: Accountability means owning results, including failures. Delegation is assigning work, which is not what the scenario describes.

questions.q: Which management function involves setting goals and deciding the course of action needed to reach them?
questions.explain: Planning sets objectives and the actions to reach them. Organizing arranges resources once the plan exists.

questions.q: A manager picks the first option that meets minimum requirements instead of searching for the best possible option. Which decision approach is this?
questions.explain: Satisficing accepts an option that is good enough. Maximizing would require evaluating all alternatives for the best one.

questions.q: Which communication barrier occurs when a receiver filters a message through personal biases and experiences?
questions.explain: Perception barriers distort meaning based on the receiver's own frame of reference. Noise refers to physical or environmental interference.

questions.q: Which ethical framework judges an action by whether it produces the greatest good for the greatest number of people?
questions.explain: Utilitarianism weighs outcomes for the largest group. Deontology judges actions by duties and rules regardless of outcomes.

questions.q: In a functional organizational structure, employees are grouped primarily by:
choices: Customer group, such as retail or business
Geographic region, such as East or West
Product line, such as snacks or drinks
Specialty, such as marketing or finance
questions.explain: Functional structures group staff by specialty. Divisional structures group by product, region, or customer.

questions.q: Which conflict management style sets aside one's own concerns to satisfy the other party and preserve the relationship?
questions.explain: Accommodating yields to the other party's wishes to protect the relationship. Competing pursues one's own goals at the other party's expense, and collaborating looks for a win-win.

questions.q: In Herzberg's two-factor theory, which of the following is a motivator rather than a hygiene factor?
questions.explain: Motivators such as achievement and recognition drive satisfaction. Hygiene factors such as salary and security prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate on their own.

questions.q: Which type of communication flows from subordinates up to managers?
questions.explain: Upward communication carries feedback, questions, and reports from staff to management. Grapevine is informal and moves in all directions.

questions.q: Controlling as a management function primarily involves:
choices: Recruiting, hiring, and training staff for open positions
Designing the organizational chart and reporting lines
Setting the long-range vision and goals for the company
Comparing actual performance to standards and correcting gaps
questions.explain: Controlling measures performance against standards and takes corrective action. The other options describe staffing, organizing, and planning.

questions.q: A decision matrix is used to:
choices: Show the sequence of tasks in a project
Trace the root causes of a problem
questions.explain: A decision matrix scores each option against weighted criteria so the totals can be compared. Forecasting, task scheduling, and root-cause analysis use other tools.

questions.q: Corporate social responsibility refers to:
choices: A company's obligations to society beyond what the law requires
Meeting only the minimum legal requirements
questions.explain: CSR covers voluntary responsibilities to employees, communities, and the environment beyond legal minimums. Doing only what the law requires is compliance, not CSR.

questions.q: Organizational culture is best described as:
choices: The legal structure of the business
Shared values, beliefs, and norms that guide behavior
The written job descriptions of employees
The budget allocated to each department
questions.explain: Culture is the shared set of values and unwritten norms that shape how people act. Legal structure and job descriptions are formal, not cultural.

questions.q: The first step in Kotter's eight-step change model is:
questions.explain: Kotter begins by establishing urgency. Consolidating gains and anchoring changes come near the end of the model.

questions.q: Servant leadership focuses primarily on:
choices: Serving the needs of followers and the community
questions.explain: Servant leaders put the growth and needs of followers first, which is the opposite of an authority-centered style.

questions.q: McGregor's Theory X assumes that employees:
choices: Are self-directed and enjoy their work
Dislike work and must be closely supervised
Are motivated mainly by peer belonging
questions.explain: Theory X is the pessimistic view that workers avoid work and need control. Theory Y is the optimistic counterpart.

questions.q: Which nonverbal cue most often signals openness and engagement during a presentation?
choices: Eye contact and an open posture
questions.explain: Eye contact and open posture show confidence and engagement. Crossed arms and distracted behavior signal the opposite.

questions.q: Span of control refers to:
choices: The number of levels in an organization
The total budget of a department
The distance between headquarters and branch offices
The number of subordinates a manager directly supervises
questions.explain: Span of control is the number of direct reports. A narrow span usually creates more management levels.

questions.q: An analysis shows that 80 percent of customer complaints come from 20 percent of causes. This pattern is known as:
questions.explain: The Pareto principle (the 80/20 rule) says a small share of causes drives most results, so it is used to prioritize problems. The Peter principle is about promotion to incompetence, and Parkinson's law says work expands to fill the time available.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a conflict of interest?
choices: A disagreement between coworkers over project timelines
Two employees whose working styles clash on an assignment
A personal interest that could improperly sway professional judgment
A task that two departments are jointly responsible for
questions.explain: A conflict of interest exists when a personal interest could compromise professional duties, even if no wrong is done.

questions.q: A matrix organizational structure is characterized by:
choices: A single chain of command with no shared authority
Employees reporting to both a functional manager and a project manager
All decisions made by one owner
questions.explain: Matrix structures give staff two reporting lines, which supports cross-functional projects but can create role confusion.

questions.q: Which is the most effective first step in resolving a workplace conflict?
choices: Have both parties present their sides at the next team meeting
Wait to see whether the problem resolves on its own
Side with the more senior employee to end it quickly
Meet privately with each party to understand the issue
questions.explain: A private conversation with each party gathers facts and keeps the issue contained before escalation is considered. Airing it in front of the team, waiting, or siding by seniority tends to harden positions.

questions.q: Which trait describes a leader's ability to remain effective when priorities change suddenly?
questions.explain: Adaptability is the capacity to adjust approach and priorities as conditions change. Conscientiousness is dependability, assertiveness is stating needs directly, and empathy is understanding how others feel.

questions.q: Vroom's expectancy theory states that motivation depends on which three factors?
questions.explain: Expectancy (effort leads to performance), instrumentality (performance leads to reward), and valence (value of the reward) multiply to produce motivation.

questions.q: Which approach best encourages participation from quieter team members during a meeting?
choices: Calling on the most senior person first only
Ending the meeting early if discussion slows
questions.explain: Round-robin turns give every member a structured chance to contribute, which draws out quieter voices.

questions.q: Which management function involves assigning people and resources to tasks and positions?
questions.explain: Organizing arranges people, tasks, and resources into a structure. Leading is about influencing and motivating people.

questions.q: Groupthink is best described as:
choices: A group decision process that suppresses dissent in pursuit of consensus
Independent decision making by each team member
questions.explain: Groupthink happens when the desire for harmony overrides critical evaluation of alternatives.

questions.q: Which principle means treating all employees fairly and giving each the opportunity to succeed based on merit and need?
questions.explain: Equity focuses on fair treatment and outcomes. Equality gives everyone the same resources, which is a related but different idea.

questions.q: Which is an example of an informal organization?
choices: The official chart showing who reports to whom
Coworkers who lunch together and swap news outside official channels
The written employee handbook of workplace policies
The board of directors elected to oversee strategy
questions.explain: The informal organization is the network of relationships that exists alongside the formal structure.

questions.q: Lewin's three-stage model of change consists of:
questions.explain: Unfreeze prepares people to let go of old behavior, change moves them to the new state, and refreeze locks in the new norm.

questions.q: Transformational leaders primarily influence followers by:
choices: Inspiring a shared vision and encouraging personal growth
Relying on rewards and punishments for compliance
Restricting information to protect their authority
questions.explain: Transformational leaders motivate through vision, inspiration, and development. Rewards and punishments describe transactional leadership.

questions.q: In Maslow's hierarchy, which need comes directly above safety needs?
questions.explain: The order from bottom to top is physiological, safety, belonging and love, esteem, and self-actualization.

questions.q: Which communication channel is best for sensitive, complex, or emotionally charged messages?
choices: Email sent to the whole department
Memo posted on the staff board
questions.explain: Face-to-face communication carries tone and nonverbal cues that reduce misunderstanding in difficult messages.

questions.q: A manager sets a quarterly budget and then compares actual spending to it each month. Which two functions are involved?
questions.explain: Setting the budget is planning. Monitoring and comparing against it is controlling.

questions.q: Which step comes first in the rational decision-making model?
questions.explain: The rational model begins with defining the problem clearly before generating or evaluating options.

questions.q: A manager discovers that a subordinate has falsified expense reports. The most ethical first response is to:
choices: Confront the employee in front of the team to deter others
Have the employee quietly repay the money and drop the matter
Investigate through proper channels and follow company policy
Fire the employee on the spot before gathering the facts
questions.explain: Ethical handling means verifying facts and following established policy and reporting channels, with due process for the employee. A quiet repayment deal hides misconduct the company may need to address, and public confrontation or instant firing skips due process.

questions.q: Centralized decision making means:
choices: Decisions are made at lower levels by front-line staff
Decisions are concentrated at the top of the organization
Every department votes on each decision
Decisions are made by outside consultants
questions.explain: Centralization keeps authority at the top. Decentralization pushes it down the hierarchy.

questions.q: Which conflict management style seeks a solution that fully satisfies both parties?
questions.explain: Collaborating, also called integrative problem solving, looks for win-win outcomes that meet both sets of interests.

questions.q: Which best describes an effective leader's vision?
choices: A clear, inspiring picture of where the group is headed
A detailed list of daily procedures and work rules
A one-year budget with spending targets
A ranked list of employee performance scores
questions.explain: A vision gives people a clear, motivating destination. Procedures, budgets, and performance rankings are operational tools, not a vision.

questions.q: Which theory proposes that people are motivated by a strong need for achievement, power, and affiliation?
questions.explain: McClelland's needs theory identifies achievement, power, and affiliation as learned needs that drive behavior.

questions.q: Which barrier to communication is caused by a lack of shared language or excessive jargon?
questions.explain: Semantic barriers arise when words mean different things to the sender and receiver.

questions.q: Which tool breaks a project into tasks, durations, and dependencies on a timeline?
questions.explain: A Gantt chart displays scheduled tasks as bars on a timeline. A fishbone diagram identifies causes of a problem.

questions.q: Which technique generates many ideas before any are evaluated?
questions.explain: Brainstorming separates idea generation from evaluation to encourage a wide range of options.

questions.q: Whistleblower protection is best described as:
choices: A bonus paid for reporting competitors
Legal safeguards for employees who report illegal or unethical conduct
A requirement to report all coworkers' personal conduct
questions.explain: Whistleblower protections shield employees from retaliation when they report wrongdoing in good faith.

questions.q: When a company removes several layers of middle management to create a flatter structure, which change usually follows?
choices: Each remaining manager supervises fewer people
Each remaining manager supervises more people
Decisions must pass through more levels of approval
The chain of command becomes longer
questions.explain: Flattening removes layers, so the remaining managers take on wider spans of control and decisions move faster. Fewer reports per manager, more approval levels, and a longer chain of command describe a tall structure.

questions.q: Resistance to change is most effectively reduced by:
choices: Announcing the change by email once every decision is final
Rolling it out quickly so there is less time to object
Limiting discussion of the change to senior managers
Involving employees early and explaining the reasons
questions.explain: Participation and clear reasoning build buy-in. Late announcements, rushed rollouts, and keeping discussion at the top tend to increase resistance.

questions.q: Situational leadership theory suggests that:
choices: The best leadership style depends on followers' readiness and the situation
One proven leadership style works best in every situation
Effective leaders are born with traits that cannot be developed
Followers should adapt their behavior to the leader's fixed style
questions.explain: Hersey and Blanchard's model matches directive or supportive behavior to follower competence and commitment.

questions.q: Which motivational approach ties rewards directly to individual performance?
questions.explain: Merit pay links compensation to measured individual results, which is a direct extrinsic reward.

questions.q: Which is the best use of feedback in a team?
choices: Focus comments on the person's personality traits
Give specific, timely feedback on behavior and results
Save feedback for the annual review so it is complete
Give only positive feedback to protect morale
questions.explain: Effective feedback is specific, timely, and focused on behavior and results. Feedback aimed at personality, saved for once a year, or kept only positive does not help people adjust.

questions.q: Staffing as a management function includes:
choices: Recruiting, selecting, training, and developing employees
questions.explain: Staffing covers filling and developing positions with qualified people.

questions.q: Which decision tool compares expected monetary outcomes weighted by their probabilities?
questions.explain: Expected value multiplies each outcome by its probability and sums the results to compare options under uncertainty.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects stakeholder theory?
choices: Managers should answer only to the shareholders who own the firm
A business's only social duty is to increase its profits
A business should weigh the interests of all groups its actions affect
Customers are the only group whose interests a firm must weigh
questions.explain: Stakeholder theory includes employees, customers, suppliers, communities, and owners, not shareholders alone. The profit-only view is shareholder theory.

questions.q: Which diagram shows job titles, reporting relationships, and lines of authority in a company?
questions.explain: An organizational chart shows the formal structure of authority and reporting. A Gantt chart shows a schedule, a flowchart shows process steps, and a Pareto chart ranks causes by frequency.

questions.q: In change management, which step reinforces new behaviors so they become the standard?
questions.explain: Refreezing in Lewin's model locks in the new behavior through reinforcement, policies, and culture.

questions.q: Which leadership quality is most closely tied to earning trust over time?
choices: Charisma and a polished public image
Tight control over what information is shared
questions.explain: Trust grows when leaders act consistently with their stated values over time. Charisma and speeches can draw attention, but they do not build trust when actions do not match words.

questions.q: Equity theory predicts that employees become dissatisfied when they perceive:
choices: Their pay is above the industry average
Their input-to-outcome ratio is unfair compared with peers
questions.explain: Equity theory compares a person's inputs and outcomes with those of comparable others. Perceived unfairness reduces motivation.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of an agenda in a business meeting?
choices: To record decisions after the meeting
To outline topics and goals in advance
To assign blame for missed deadlines
questions.explain: An agenda sets topics, goals, and timing so participants can prepare and the meeting stays focused.

questions.q: A restaurant manager inspects every produce delivery and rejects damaged items before they reach the kitchen. Which type of control is this?
questions.explain: Feedforward (preventive) control catches problems at the input stage, before work begins. Concurrent control happens during the work, and feedback control happens after results are in.

questions.q: In a SWOT analysis, a new competitor entering the market and a rise in the minimum wage are best classified as:
questions.explain: Both are external conditions that could hurt the business, which makes them threats. Strengths and weaknesses are internal factors, and opportunities are favorable external conditions.

questions.q: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 primarily aimed to:
choices: Regulate interest rates and fees on consumer credit cards
Raise the federal minimum wage for hourly workers
Improve corporate financial disclosure and accountability
Protect workers' rights to form and join labor unions
questions.explain: SOX was a U.S. federal response to corporate accounting scandals, and it strengthened internal controls and executive responsibility.

questions.q: A consumer goods company runs its snack, beverage, and personal care businesses as separate units, each with its own marketing, production, and finance teams. Which structure is this?
questions.explain: Divisional structures organize around products, markets, or regions, and each division has its own functional resources. A functional structure would put all marketing in one department across every product.

questions.q: Which is a common driver of organizational change?
choices: A stable customer base with steady demand
New technology or shifting market demand
questions.explain: External forces such as new technology and market shifts are a main reason organizations must change. Stable demand, traditions, and low turnover tend to favor the status quo.

questions.q: Which is the best definition of leadership?
choices: The process of influencing a group toward achieving goals
The formal authority to give orders to subordinates
The job title held by a senior manager or executive
The power to reward and punish employee behavior
questions.explain: Leadership is influence. Authority, titles, and the power to reward or punish do not guarantee that people will follow.

questions.q: A company raises pay and improves office conditions, but employees say they feel no more motivated than before. Herzberg's two-factor theory explains this because pay and working conditions are:
choices: Motivators that take a year to have an effect
Hygiene factors that prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate
Valences that only matter to top performers
questions.explain: Herzberg classed pay, policy, supervision, and working conditions as hygiene factors: improving them removes dissatisfaction, but motivation comes from motivators such as achievement and recognition.

questions.q: A manager receives a message full of technical jargon from a remote team. Which step best ensures understanding?
choices: Reply using the same technical terms to show expertise
Paraphrase it back and ask the team to confirm
Wait until the next team meeting to ask about it
Forward it to a senior executive to interpret
questions.explain: Paraphrasing and asking for confirmation closes the feedback loop and catches misunderstandings early.

questions.q: Delegation means:
choices: Assigning all tasks to the most senior staff
Doing all the work personally to ensure quality
Assigning tasks and authority while keeping accountability for outcomes
questions.explain: Delegation transfers authority for a task, but the manager remains accountable for results.

questions.q: Which bias occurs when people favor information that supports their existing beliefs?
questions.explain: Confirmation bias leads decision makers to seek and weigh evidence that confirms what they already think.

questions.q: Which principle means a company discloses material information fairly and truthfully to stakeholders?
questions.explain: Transparency means open, accurate disclosure. Confidentiality protects information, which can be appropriate but is a different principle.

questions.q: In a span of control analysis, a narrow span usually means:
questions.explain: A narrow span means each manager supervises few people, which usually creates more layers in a tall structure.

questions.q: Which phase of Tuckman's model of team development features members testing roles and disagreeing?
questions.explain: Storming is the conflict phase. Forming is orientation, norming is agreement on norms, and performing is productive work.

questions.q: Which leadership approach gives followers the most freedom with the least direction?
questions.explain: Laissez-faire leaders step back and let the group decide and self-manage.

questions.q: A sales rep makes no effort toward a quarterly bonus because she believes no amount of work will let her hit the target. In Vroom's expectancy theory, which element is low?
questions.explain: Expectancy is the belief that effort will lead to the required performance. Instrumentality is the belief that performance will bring the reward, and valence is how much the reward is valued.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of an elevator pitch?
choices: To close a sale on the spot before the listener leaves
To quickly explain who you are and what you offer
To present a full business plan in detail
To negotiate salary and benefits with an employer
questions.explain: An elevator pitch is a short, clear introduction. It is meant to spark interest, not to close a deal.

questions.q: Which management function is primarily about influencing and motivating people toward goals?
questions.explain: Leading covers motivation, direction, and communication to align people with goals.

questions.q: A decision tree is most useful for:
choices: Mapping sequential choices and their possible outcomes
Scheduling project tasks along a timeline
Sorting the causes of a problem into categories
questions.explain: Decision trees branch by choice and chance to show possible paths and outcomes for a decision. Reporting lines belong on an organizational chart, timelines on a Gantt chart, and cause categories on a fishbone diagram.

questions.q: Which situation is an example of a conflict of interest for a purchasing agent?
choices: Approving a contract with a supplier owned by a relative
questions.explain: A relationship with the supplier could bias the purchasing decision, which is what makes it a conflict of interest.

questions.q: Organizational culture is most often passed on to new employees through:
choices: Formal job descriptions and duty lists
Stories, rituals, and observed leader behavior
The organizational chart and job titles
questions.explain: Culture is learned through stories, ceremonies, and what leaders model and reward. Job descriptions, financial reports, and the org chart describe the formal organization, not its unwritten norms.

questions.q: Which change management practice matters most when introducing new software?
choices: Switching every department over on the same day to save time
Letting each employee learn the software on their own
Announcing the switch on the day it goes live
Providing training and support before and after launch
questions.explain: User adoption depends on training and ongoing support, which is a core change management principle. Rushed switchovers, self-teaching, and last-minute announcements raise errors and resistance.

questions.q: Which leadership quality describes holding oneself to a clear code of conduct even when no one is watching?
questions.explain: Integrity is consistent ethical conduct regardless of observation.

questions.q: An employee worried about losing her job in upcoming layoffs is focused on which level of Maslow's hierarchy?
questions.explain: Job security is a classic safety need, the level just above basic physiological needs such as food and shelter.

questions.q: What is the best way to close a presentation?
choices: Thank the audience and stop after the last data slide
Summarize the key points and state the call to action
Introduce a new topic to keep interest high
Apologize for running over time and stop
questions.explain: A strong close summarizes the main message and tells the audience what to do next. Ending on raw data, adding new material, or apologizing weakens the final impression.

questions.q: Which tool compares actual results against standards to find and explain gaps?
questions.explain: Variance analysis calculates the difference between planned and actual results and investigates the cause.

questions.q: A team keeps missing shipping deadlines and wants to trace the problem to its root causes by sorting possible causes into categories such as people, methods, materials, and machines. Which tool fits best?
questions.explain: A fishbone (Ishikawa, or cause-and-effect) diagram sorts the possible causes of a problem into categories so the team can find root causes. A Gantt chart schedules tasks, a decision tree compares choices, and SWOT assesses strategic position.

questions.q: Which statement best describes fiduciary duty?
choices: A duty to maximize personal bonuses
A duty to avoid all risk
A legal obligation to act in the best interest of another party
A duty to share profits equally with employees
questions.explain: Fiduciaries such as directors and trustees must put the interests of the party they serve ahead of their own.

questions.q: A line-and-staff structure differs from a pure line structure because it adds:
questions.explain: Staff specialists advise line managers, who keep command authority over operations.

questions.q: Which best describes organizational resilience?
choices: Keeping the same structure and processes regardless of conditions
The ability to grow faster than competitors
Avoiding risk by never entering new markets
The ability to adapt to and recover from disruption
questions.explain: Resilience is the capacity to absorb shocks, adapt, and recover while continuing core operations. Rigidity and risk avoidance reduce resilience, and growth speed is a different measure.

questions.q: Emotional intelligence in leadership most directly involves:
choices: Recognizing and managing your own and others' emotions
Keeping emotions out of every workplace conversation
Making decisions based on logic and data alone
Reading body language to tell when people are lying
questions.explain: Emotional intelligence includes self-awareness, self-management, empathy, and relationship skills.

questions.q: Which type of reward is intrinsic?
choices: A year-end bonus for meeting sales targets
A promotion that comes with a higher salary
A gift card from the manager for good work
questions.explain: Intrinsic rewards come from within the person, such as a sense of accomplishment. Pay and gifts are extrinsic.

questions.q: In negotiation, which approach focuses on mutual gain rather than winning at the other party's expense?
questions.explain: Integrative negotiation expands value by exploring interests, which creates outcomes both sides can accept.

questions.q: Which is an example of the organizing function?
choices: Setting a five-year sales growth goal
Monitoring monthly sales against the budget
Motivating a team with a pep talk
Creating a department with clear reporting lines
questions.explain: Creating departments and reporting lines is organizing. The other options are planning, controlling, and leading.

questions.q: Which decision-making model assumes complete information and a fully logical process?
questions.explain: The rational model assumes full information and optimal choice. The garbage can and satisficing models relax those assumptions.

questions.q: Which best describes a code of ethics?
choices: A list of workplace rules on attendance and dress
A written statement of values and standards of conduct
A contract guaranteeing employees job security
questions.explain: A code of ethics states the values and expected conduct for members of an organization. Attendance and dress rules belong in an employee handbook.

questions.q: A bank organizes its staff into separate units for retail customers, small businesses, and large corporations. Which type of departmentalization is this?
questions.explain: Customer departmentalization groups work around the needs of distinct customer segments. Functional groups by specialty, geographic by location, and process by stage of work.

questions.q: Which concept describes employees' initial reluctance to new processes?
questions.explain: Resistance to change is the natural reluctance to give up familiar routines and is a normal part of change management.

questions.q: A leader uses 360-degree feedback primarily to:
choices: Gather input from peers, direct reports, and supervisors for development
Rate employees using only their direct supervisor's view
Compare each employee's sales with company averages
Collect customer ratings of the company's products
questions.explain: 360-degree feedback collects input from every direction around the person to support self-awareness and development. A single supervisor's rating is a traditional review.

questions.q: A manager lets her team set their own weekly targets, asks for their ideas, and checks in rather than monitoring them constantly. Which set of assumptions does her approach reflect?
questions.explain: Theory Y assumes people can be self-directed and seek responsibility, so managers give autonomy and invite input. Theory X and scientific management assume close supervision and control are needed.

questions.q: Which is the best example of active listening?
choices: Planning your reply while the other person speaks
Restating the speaker's point to confirm understanding
Interrupting to share your own experience
Offering a solution as soon as you spot the problem
questions.explain: Active listening includes paraphrasing and checking understanding. Planning a reply, interrupting, or jumping straight to solutions shifts the focus away from the speaker.

questions.q: A manager tracks weekly output against a target and adjusts staffing when output falls short. Which two functions are primarily involved?
questions.explain: Tracking against the target is controlling, and changing staffing levels and assignments is organizing.

vocab.def: The process of influencing a group of people toward achieving a common goal.
A leadership style in which the leader inspires followers through a shared vision and encourages their development.
A leadership style based on exchanges, where rewards and penalties are tied to performance.
A leadership approach that puts the needs and growth of followers and the community first.
A leadership style in which the leader makes decisions alone with little input from members.
A leadership style in which members participate in decision making, with the leader guiding the group.
A hands-off leadership style in which members are given wide freedom to make decisions.
The ability to recognize and manage one's own emotions and to understand and respond to the emotions of others.
A theory that ranks human needs from physiological to self-actualization, with lower needs generally met first.
A theory that separates hygiene factors, which prevent dissatisfaction, from motivators, which create satisfaction.
McGregor's view that workers dislike work, avoid responsibility, and must be closely directed and controlled.
McGregor's view that workers can be self-directed, seek responsibility, and be committed when conditions allow.
A motivation theory holding that effort depends on the belief that effort leads to performance and performance leads to valued rewards.
A motivation theory holding that people judge fairness by comparing their input-to-outcome ratio with that of others.
Motivation that comes from within a person, such as enjoyment of the work or personal satisfaction.
Motivation driven by external rewards such as pay, promotion, or recognition.
A communication technique in which the listener concentrates fully on the speaker and confirms understanding by paraphrasing.
Information about performance or behavior given to a person so they can understand results and adjust.
The transmission of meaning through body language, facial expression, eye contact, and tone of voice rather than words.
A communication barrier created when the sender and receiver attach different meanings to the same words or jargon.
Communication that flows from subordinates to managers, such as reports, suggestions, and questions.
The informal communication network through which information spreads among employees outside official channels.
A model of team growth in four stages: forming, storming, norming, and performing (later adding adjourning).
The management function of setting goals and determining the actions needed to achieve them.
The management function of arranging people, tasks, and resources into a structure that supports the plan.
The management function of influencing and motivating people to work toward organizational goals.
The management function of measuring performance against standards and taking corrective action when needed.
Assigning tasks and the authority to complete them to another person while the delegator stays accountable for results.
The number of employees a manager directly supervises.
The management function of recruiting, selecting, training, and developing employees.
A group technique for generating many ideas quickly, with evaluation deferred until after idea generation.
A decision approach that selects the first option that meets minimum acceptable criteria rather than the best possible option.
